writeup.1: The wedge is the only club most golfers will ever have marked with their own name, and a small industry has grown up around that. It runs from a man in Gilbert, Arizona who takes the head off your Vokey so the shaft never sees heat, through Japanese forging houses that will hand-grind a sole to your attack angle, up to a Callaway employee in Carlsbad whose work sits in the bags of two former presidents and cannot be bought at any price.
writeup.2: It also runs through a lot of drop-down menus. Only a handful of these makers do one-off work: Show Out and the other independent engravers, Artisan in Fort Worth, KYOEI’s custom programme, and Anthony Taranto, whose wedges are not for sale. Grindworks, Fourteen, Bettinardi, Edel, New Level, Indi and Miura all label their wedges custom, and all of them mean built-to-order from a fixed set of options. Built-to-order is a good way to buy a wedge, but it is not bespoke, and the word custom covers both without telling you which one you are getting.
writeup.3: Thirty-two wedges from eleven makers come first, then every manufacturer program set against what it publishes about its own limits. Prices sit in the currency the seller prints, and where a seller prints no currency at all — KYOEI does not, anywhere on its site — the number appears exactly as they show it.
